newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - August 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - August 1.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- PENGUIN MANAGER'S IMMUNITY CLAUSE

It emerged on Thursday that Penguin USA's account manager, Christina Galatro, currently defending herself against accusations of embezzling $1.4 million from the book publisher, received a severance package from the group upon her sacking in February. The package released Galatro from any responsibilities connected with an accounting error that led to a 100 million stg charge at Penguin's parent company, Pearson. Penguin officials refused to comment on the severance agreement, but said they stood by the lawsuit.
-- KENWOOD 221,000 stg to FORMER MD

Kitchen appliances group Kenwood Appliances has revealed it paid 221,000 stg in compensation to former managing director Tim Beech upon his resignation in January. The company later went on to report an 11.4 million stg loss in the year to April, following an exceptional reorganisation charge of 15.5 million stg, compared with a 15.6 million stg pre-tax profit in 1996. Beech was later replaced by former Grand Met employee Colin Gordon, who received 15,500 stg for his first month.
-- GRAND MET CHIEF WANTS TO RESTART LVMH DIALOGUE

Grand Metropolitan chief John McGrath has indicated he believes Guiness and Grand Met should resume talks with Bernard Arnault's LVMH, who is still seeking to block the merger between the two and was in London on Thursday pleading his cause. McGrath stressed the need for all three groups to exercise "patience" in their search for "areas of common ground". Meetings between the three are yet to be planned.
THE TIMES
-- SIMON BREAKS SILENCE ON SHARES ROW

Lord Simon, the controversial Labour MP who holds two million stg worth of BP shares, is to defend his shareholding against Tory accusations of conflict of interest on Friday. Simon has stated the accusations are unfounded, untrue and absurd, and could contribute to making other businessmen
wary of becoming involved with the government.
-- CAPITAL BID FOR VIRGIN TRANSMITTED TO MMC

UK competition and consumer affairs minister Nigel Griffiths has referred the 64.7 million stg offer by Capital Radio for Richard Branson's Virgin Radio to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. The offer was earlier waived through by the radio industry regulator for fear it would give Capital a dominant share of the market for radio advertising in London. The MMC is
expected to report in November.
-- CITY ANGRY AT BT'S SILENCE OVER MCI MERGER

Sir Peter Bonfield, British Telecom's chief executive, has further angered London analysts and investors following his decision to maintain a "wall of silence" over the company's 12 billion stg merger with MCI. BT investors had expected some news from Sir Peter, as MCI released its first-quarter results on Thursday, but Sir Peter declined to comment on the progress of price negotiations or even how much scope there was to redraft the contract.
THE GUARDIAN
-- PRIVACY CLAMP ON THE MEDIA

On Thursday, the Home Office published plans for a comprehensive reform concerning the use of personal information, which will lead to the first-ever statutory right of privacy in Britain. The proposals cover "the processing of personal data", access to ones own personal data, safeguards covering the use of sensitive information and rules governing the media's balance of private information with the public's right to know. The proposals include exemptions for police and security services.
-- BALLPOINT PEN MAKER BIC PICKS UP SHEAFFER FOR 30M

French-based Societe Bic, the company famous for its basic ball point pens, has acquired US luxury pen manufacturer Sheaffer, whose top of the line pens sell for up to 3,000 stg. Bic is to pay around 30 million stg for Sheaffer in a move that should help it gain access to the elite side of the market and help lift revenue by more than 35 million stg.
-- OUTPUT CUT IN OIFIELDS

Falling oil prices, the strength of sterling and a decline in seasonal output have led to revenues from North Sea oil and gas fields falling to their lowest in more than two years. Latest figures from the Royal Bank of Scotland's monthly oil and gas index illustrate that the average price of Brent crude in June fell eight percent to $17.70, with oil output 12 percent lower than in May and gas input down by almost 10 percent.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- IT WILL BE GOOD TO TALK, SHOP, BANK WITH FUTURE MOBILE

On Thursday, trade and industry minister Barbara Roche outlined plans for the third wave of licensing for the radio spectrum, which will lead to the creation of a new range of high-tech services, such as mobile phones that offer everything from Internet access to home shopping. Licences for the new bandwaves will be auctioned off prior to April 1999, with
services set to begin in 2002.
-- RONSON RECEIVES TAKEOVER APPROACH FROM MYSTERY BIDDER

Lighters to branded clothes group Ronson has revealed it has been approached with a hostile takeover bid, but would not disclose who had made the bid other than to say it was not recently ousted chief executive Howard Hodgson. The news led share prices in the group to rise 2.5p to 21p, with insiders tipping US-based Albion Consortium as the possible bidder as it presently holds an 18 percent stake in Ronson.
-- ROYAL DOULTON TO CUT 330 JOBS

Royal Doulton, the fine china group, has announced it will axe 330 jobs as part of its endeavours to become more competitive and battle problems brought on by the strength of sterling. The majority of job losses will come at the group's nine Stoke-on-Trent plants, 270 of which will emanate from the production, clerical and commercial divisions. New chief executive Peter Wegner has not ruled out the possibility of future job cuts.
